name: Diagnose and sign out surgical pathology and referred cytology cases
summary: Anatomic pathologists examine the slides of each biopsy or referred cytology case with its history, decide whether they can diagnose it or need deeper levels, special stains, immunohistochemistry, a colleague's opinion or more clinical information, then dictate the diagnosis for a medical transcriptionist to type and sign the report electronically. Most community biopsies are signed out in one or two days, but immunohistochemistry, consultations and outside opinions add days and the case waits at several queues: the pathologist's tray, transcription and signature. Errors are mostly misinterpretations and report defects such as wrong sites or typing errors, and about five reports in a thousand are later amended.

baseline.org_archetype: A large Canadian community laboratory company with about 45 anatomic pathologists reporting community biopsies and referred cytology, using an anatomic pathology system with dictation and transcription.
baseline.notes: About 13,000 surgical cases and 4,100 referred cytology cases a month reach the pathologists; subspecialty work includes dermatopathology, gastrointestinal, uropathology, breast and gynaecologic pathology.

trigger: Slides of a surgical case from histology, or a referred cytology case from the cytotechnologists, reach the pathologist's worklist.
end_state: The pathologist signs the report, which is released to the LIS for delivery to the clinician, and the slides are filed.

volume.seasonality: Follows biopsy and Pap volumes; lower in summer and holiday weeks.

evidence.note: Organisation file estimate; the companion workflows imply about 17,000 a month, inside the range.

More than 60 pathologists with listed subspecialties; FTE derived from minutes times volume within the 45 anatomic pathologists. Loaded cost is hourly wage times 1.35 (benefits, payroll taxes and overhead), as in the organisation file.

systems.name: Anatomic pathology case management with dictation and synoptic reporting
Laboratory information system (orders, accessioning, results, autoverification rules)
Tissue processors, embedding centres, microtomes, stainers and coverslippers
Block and slide filing and retention storage

steps.name: Route the case to the pathologist's worklist
steps.description: When the slides arrive, the anatomic pathology system shows the case on the assigned pathologist's worklist with the requisition, gross description, prior pathology and, for cytology, the cytotechnologist's preliminary interpretation.

next.condition: cytology case referred by a cytotechnologist

evidence.note: Shares follow from about 13,000 surgical cases and 4,100 referred cytology cases a month in the companion workflows.

steps.name: Examine the surgical slides with the history
steps.description: The pathologist reads the requisition and gross description, examines every part and level under the microscope, compares with prior pathology, and decides whether the diagnosis is clear or needs deeper levels, special stains, immunohistochemistry, a colleague's opinion or more clinical information.
outputs: working diagnosis or further work order

next.condition: deeper levels or special stains needed
more tissue needed from the stored specimen

evidence.note: Second review in 6.6% of cases (median laboratory 8.2%); immunohistochemistry and consultation lengthen turnaround; other shares and minutes are estimates for community biopsies.

steps.name: Review a referred cytology case
steps.description: The pathologist reviews the dotted cells and the slide as needed with the cytotechnologist's interpretation and the patient's history, and decides the final Bethesda or descriptive category and recommendation, showing a colleague when unsure.

control.basis: A pathologist confirms every gynaecologic slide with reactive, atypical, premalignant or malignant changes (accreditation practice; stated in the US rule 42 CFR 493.1274)

evidence.note: Pathologist confirmation is described; average cytology turnaround of 1.63 days in one series; minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Cut deeper levels or special stains
steps.description: The histotechnologist retrieves the block from the file, cuts the requested levels or sections for histochemical stains such as PAS, iron or a Helicobacter stain, stains and labels them, and returns them with the case.

error.defect_description: Wrong block retrieved or slide mislabelled.

evidence.note: Recuts, deeper sections and special stains add 1 to 2 days; minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Order immunohistochemistry
steps.description: The pathologist selects the antibody panel and blocks in the anatomic pathology system, which sends the order to the immunohistochemistry laboratory, and keeps the case pending.

evidence.note: Immunohistochemistry use lengthens turnaround; minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Immunohistochemistry laboratory stains the panel
steps.description: The case waits while the separate immunohistochemistry process cuts and stains the panel and returns the slides; that work is counted in the IHC and molecular pathology workflow.

evidence.note: Special stains and immunohistochemistry add 1 to 2 working days; weekends widen the range.

steps.name: Review the additional slides
steps.description: The pathologist examines the deeper levels or special stains with the original slides and either settles the diagnosis or asks for immunohistochemistry or a colleague's opinion.

evidence.note: Shares and minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Show the case to a colleague
steps.description: A second pathologist reviews the slides and the primary pathologist's impression, gives an opinion and the consultation is recorded in the report; difficult cases may be sent to an outside expert.

control.basis: Departmental second-review policy (for example new malignancies and designated case types), recorded in the report as recommended by the University of Toronto pathology quality indicator guidelines

evidence.note: Reasons for review: difficult diagnosis 46.2%, departmental policy 43.0%; 78% involve one additional pathologist; consultation adds 1 to 2 days.

steps.name: Prepare the case for outside consultation
steps.description: The medical transcriptionist prepares the consultation letter and copies of the requisition and report draft, the slides and blocks are pulled and packaged, and the courier shipment is logged on the pending list.

evidence.note: Preparing consultation reports and tracking incoming and outgoing reports are listed duties; minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Outside expert reviews the case
steps.description: The expert pathologist at an academic centre reviews the slides and returns a written consultation by courier, fax or email.

evidence.note: Three days to two weeks is an estimate.

steps.name: Request missing clinical information
steps.description: The medical transcriptionist phones or faxes the ordering physician's office for the clinical history or the biopsy site the pathologist needs and notes the request on the case.

evidence.note: Common practice; minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Physician's office supplies the history
steps.description: The office calls back or faxes the missing history, site or clinical question and the case returns to the pathologist.

evidence.note: Response times are estimates.

steps.name: Submit more tissue from the stored specimen
steps.description: The pathologists' assistant retrieves the stored container, submits further tissue in new cassettes as the pathologist asked and records the additional sections in the gross description.

evidence.note: Resubmission of tissue adds 1 to 2 days; minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Process the new cassettes overnight
steps.description: The new cassettes go through the overnight processor with the next run before they can be embedded and cut; nobody works on them meanwhile.

evidence.note: Overnight fixation and processing add a day.

steps.name: Dictate the diagnosis
steps.description: The pathologist dictates the final diagnosis lines, microscopic description and comments into the dictation system, naming the specimen parts and any consultation.

evidence.note: Dictation with transcription was common in the period; minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Enter a coded cytology diagnosis
steps.description: The pathologist selects the Bethesda category, adequacy statement and screening recommendation from coded lists in the anatomic pathology system, adding a free-text comment when needed.

evidence.note: Common practice; minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Transcribe the dictated report
steps.description: The medical transcriptionist listens to the dictation, types the report into the case template, checks specimen sites, laterality and patient details against the requisition, and queues it for the pathologist's signature.

error.defect_description: Typing, laterality or site error in the report.

evidence.note: Transcription and proofreading are listed duties and transcription editing is a named delay point; minutes and error rate are estimates.

steps.name: Proofread and sign out the report
steps.description: The pathologist reads the transcribed or coded report against the dictation and the slides, corrects it or returns it to transcription, and signs it electronically, which releases it to the LIS for delivery.

error.defect_description: Report defect released (wrong site, typo or misidentification) and later amended.

control.basis: Pathology diagnoses are made and signed only by a licensed physician pathologist (Laboratory and Specimen Collection Centre Licensing Act licensing and CPSO or CPSM registration; accreditation report requirements); MLTs may not communicate a diagnosis

next.condition: unexpected or urgent finding to phone

evidence.note: 4.7 report defects per 1,000 cases (median 5.7) with 58.4% nondiagnostic; pathologist verification is a named delay point; the return share is an estimate.

steps.name: Phone the clinician about an unexpected finding
steps.description: For an unexpected malignancy, infection or other significant finding the pathologist phones the ordering clinician, confirms who received the result and documents the call in the report.

control.basis: Critical and significant unexpected findings policy: document what was communicated, when and to whom

evidence.note: A critical results list and documentation of communication are recommended; share and minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Return slides and paperwork to the file
steps.description: The histology laboratory assistant collects the signed-out cases, files the slides by case number for retention and files or scans the paperwork.

evidence.note: Common practice; minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Review the IHC slides and integrate the result
steps.description: The pathologist examines the stained panel with the original slides, interprets each marker, and settles the diagnosis or asks a colleague.

evidence.note: Minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Dictate the integrated report
steps.description: The pathologist dictates the diagnosis together with the immunohistochemistry results and an interpretive comment, listing each marker, its staining pattern and what it supports or excludes.

evidence.note: Minutes are estimates.

steps.name: Transcribe the integrated report
steps.description: The medical transcriptionist types the longer report with its marker table, checks it against the requisition and queues it for signature.

evidence.note: Minutes and error rate are estimates.

steps.name: Proofread and sign out the integrated report
steps.description: The pathologist checks the transcribed report, corrects it and signs it electronically, which releases it to the LIS for delivery.

error.defect_description: Report defect released and later amended.

control.basis: Pathology diagnoses are made and signed only by a licensed physician pathologist (Laboratory and Specimen Collection Centre Licensing Act licensing and CPSO or CPSM registration; accreditation report requirements); MLTs may not communicate a diagnosis

evidence.note: Report defects are described; minutes are estimates.

exceptions.name: Deeper levels or special stains
exceptions.description: Blocks are recut or stained and the case waits about a day.

exceptions.name: Immunohistochemistry
exceptions.description: The case waits one to three days for the IHC laboratory and gets a longer integrated report.

exceptions.name: Intradepartmental consultation
exceptions.description: A second pathologist reviews the case before sign-out.

exceptions.name: Outside expert consultation
exceptions.description: Slides go to an academic expert and the case waits days to weeks.

exceptions.name: Missing clinical information
exceptions.description: The transcriptionist asks the office for the history before the pathologist can finish.

exceptions.name: Report returned for corrections
exceptions.description: The pathologist returns the transcribed report for corrections before signing.

exceptions.name: Amended report after sign-out
exceptions.description: A defect found after release (typo, site, misidentification or misinterpretation) leads to an amended report in the result reporting process.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from slides on the worklist to signed report
benchmarks.population: Author's estimate for community biopsies and referred cytology

evidence.note: Derived from total accession-to-report benchmarks (CAP 90% of routine biopsies within 2 working days, average 1.48 days for biopsies in hospitalist19, 85.9% by the second working day in epmc_tat) less about one day for histology.

benchmarks.unit: percent of biopsy diagnoses signed out by the second working day
benchmarks.population: 5,384 biopsies in 157 small hospitals (Novis et al. 1998)

benchmarks.unit: percent of surgical cases reviewed by a second pathologist

pain_points.description: Dictation and transcription add a queue and a round trip before signature, and transcription editing and pathologist verification are named delay points.
Immunohistochemistry and consultations add one to three days and drive the slow tail of turnaround.
Missing clinical history on requisitions sends cases back to the physician's office.

evidence.note: Common practice.

pain_points.description: Report defects, most of them nondiagnostic (wrong site, typing, demographics), lead to amended reports after release.

evidence.note: 58.4% of defects are nondiagnostic.

sources.title: Europe PMC record: Nakhleh et al. 2010, Surgical pathology case reviews before sign-out (Q-Probes study of 45 laboratories)
sources.publisher: Europe PMC (abstract of Archives of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine)
sources.supports: 1,183 of 18,032 cases (6.6%) reviewed by a second pathologist before sign-out, median laboratory 8.2%; reasons: difficult diagnosis 46.2%, departmental policy 43.0%; 78% involved one additional pathologist; laboratories with review policies reviewed 9.6% versus 6.5%.

sources.title: Europe PMC records: surgical pathology turnaround studies (Volmar et al. 2015; Alshieban and Al-Surimi 2015; Patel et al. 2012; Novis et al. 1998)
sources.supports: Novis 1998: 85.9% of 5,384 biopsy diagnoses signed out by the second working day in 157 small hospitals; Patel 2012: 77% of non-biopsy cases within 2 days, with consultation, immunohistochemistry, malignancy and number of slides lengthening turnaround; Alshieban 2015: about 24% of routine cases missed the 2-day standard, delays at slide delivery, slide review, transcription editing and pathologist verification; Volmar 2015: median 2.72 days for large or complex specimens.

sources.title: How long should it take to get a pathology diagnosis? (Manivel et al., AVAHO 2019 abstract)
sources.supports: CAP: 90% of routine biopsies finalised within 2 working days; ADASP: at least 80% within 3 days; in 31,407 biopsies (2016 to 2018) average turnaround was 1.48 days for all biopsies and 2.2 days for biopsies with a new malignancy; 6.41% of biopsies were new malignancies; average 1.63 days for all cytologies; special stains had no significant effect on turnaround.

sources.title: Pathology quality indicator guidelines (Rowsell and Ghorab)
sources.publisher: Laboratory Medicine and Pathobiology Quality Council, University of Toronto
sources.supports: Prospective reviews with another pathologist should be recorded with the reviewer's name and scope; turnaround is more informative split into diagnostic biopsies and resections; laboratories keep a critical results list and document what was communicated, when and to whom.

sources.title: Bringing down defects in surgical pathology reports (Paxton)
sources.supports: Q-Probes study of 73 institutions and 360,218 cases: 4.7 report defects (corrected reports) per 1,000, median 5.7; earlier studies 1.4 to 4.8 per 1,000; misinterpretation 14.6%, misidentification 13.3%, specimen defects 13.7%, other nondiagnostic defects 58.4%; 24.9% found by reviewing report text after sign-out; second identifiers on 75.7% of slides and 40% of blocks; laboratories where another pathologist reviews all malignancies before sign-out had fewer misidentifications.

sources.title: Specimen turnaround time
sources.publisher: UC Davis Health, Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine
sources.supports: Biopsies 2 to 3 working days from accession; special stains and immunohistochemistry add 1 to 2 days; decalcification 1 to 2 days; intradepartmental consultation 1 to 2 days; overnight fixation 1 day; resubmission of tissue 1 to 2 days; recuts or deeper sections 1 to 2 days.

sources.title: 42 CFR 493.1274 Standard: Cytology
sources.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School
sources.supports: US rule used as a reference for common practice: review of at least 10% of negative gynaecologic cases, randomly selected and including high-risk patients, before reporting; maximum 100 slides per person per 24 hours, not a performance target, individual limits reassessed every 6 months; a pathologist confirms every gynaecologic slide with reactive, atypical, premalignant or malignant changes; five-year look-back of prior negatives for a new HSIL or cancer; comparison of HSIL cytology with histology; annual statistical evaluation; slides retained and retrievable.

sources.title: Medical Transcriptionist (Histology), Winnipeg
sources.supports: Prepare consultation reports for pathologists, track incoming and outgoing reports, turnaround-time audits and monthly report totals, surgical pathology quality assurance support; medical terminology and transcription experience, 40 words a minute, advanced proofreading.

sources.title: Medical Laboratory Technologist (Histology team), Brampton
sources.supports: Monday to Friday 3:00 p.m. to 11:00 p.m.; $35.00 to $38.75 an hour; all aspects of histology including grossing, embedding, microtomy and routine and special staining; verify sample identification; quality control and routine equipment maintenance; CMLTO registration.

sources.title: Pathology Assistant (Histology team), Brampton
sources.supports: Monday to Friday 9:00 p.m. to 5:00 a.m.; $28.00 to $30.50 an hour; gross examination of surgical specimens, selection and dissection of tissue, documentation of gross findings, embedding, positive patient identification, loading tissue processors per SOP, quality assurance.

sources.title: Hospital solutions
sources.supports: Nine Canadian laboratories, more than 60 pathologists, more than 500 hospitals served; services include pathology and histology, cytology, immunohistochemistry and microbiology; subspecialties include dermatology, gastrointestinal, breast, prostate and gynaecology.

sources.title: Licences and quality commitment
sources.supports: The quality management system uses software to monitor quality control of analytical processes, external quality assessment (CAP, QMP-LS, Healthmetrix) for all assays, internal audits and document control; Brampton, London, Ottawa and Peterborough hold ISO 15189 accreditation and Ontario licences; Winnipeg holds CAP and MANQAP accreditation for chemistry, cytology, histology, haematology and microbiology; pathology subspecialties include dermatopathology, gastrointestinal, uropathology, breast and gynaecologic pathology.

sources.title: Laws and legislation governing MLT practice
sources.publisher: College of Medical Laboratory Technologists of Ontario
sources.supports: Medical Laboratory Technology Act, 1991: the scope of practice is the performance of laboratory investigations and the evaluation of the technical sufficiency of the investigations and their results; communicating a diagnosis is not an MLT authorised act; protected title.

assumptions: The biomarker report from gs-ihc-molecular-pathology returns to a case already open here, so it carries a share of 0 in triggered_by; the IHC wait is modelled as step p06 and the IHC work belongs to that workflow.

Shares of 76% surgical and 24% cytology follow from the companion histology (13,000) and cytology (about 4,100 referred) workflows; together about 17,000 a month, against the process map's mode of 16,000.

Rates of deeper levels or special stains (13%), immunohistochemistry (7%) and missing history (2%) are the author's estimates for community biopsies; second review at 5% of first reads plus later consults gives about 6% overall, close to the 6.6% Q-Probes figure.

Pathologist minutes (about 5 minutes median microscopy for a community biopsy, 3 for referred cytology) are estimates; total stated pathologist time is about 31 FTE of the 45 anatomic pathologists, who also report hospital referral and consultation cases and do quality assurance work not modelled here.

Cases on the IHC path end with their own dictation, transcription and sign-out steps so the ihc_request output can be tied to an outcome; unexpected-finding calls on that path are not modelled separately.
Amended reports after sign-out are handled in the result reporting workflow; the defect probability at sign-out is set near the published 4.7 per 1,000.
Loaded costs are the organisation file's (hourly wage times 1.35).
